analysis.one_liner: Lets individuals, pharmacies, and wholesalers import FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada at lower prices.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let Americans buy lower-priced FDA-approved drugs from Canada, was introduced by a single sponsor with no cosponsors, never received a hearing or vote, and died in a House subcommittee in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have changed federal law to allow people to bring up to a 90-day supply of FDA-approved prescription drugs across the border from Canada for their own use, purchased from licensed Canadian pharmacies with a valid prescription. After one year, licensed pharmacies, internet pharmacies, and wholesalers could also import these drugs to sell in the U.S., with special labeling marking them as imported. The bill paired this opening with a large safety apparatus: licensing and registration of importers, internet pharmacy licensing with fees, anti-counterfeiting rules, and new FDA authority to detain or suspend risky drug shipments. Like most drug importation bills, it died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who pay U.S. retail prices for prescription drugs — especially the uninsured and people paying out of pocket — could buy the same FDA-approved drugs at Canadian prices, which are typically far lower because Canada regulates drug prices. Licensed U.S., Canadian, and internet pharmacies and wholesalers would also gain a legal market for importing and dispensing these drugs.

how_it_helps.text: It lets any individual import FDA-approved prescription drugs from Canada for personal use, up to a 90-day supply, purchased from a licensed Canadian pharmacy with a valid prescription [S2][S3].

One year after enactment, registered pharmacies, internet pharmacies, and wholesalers could import these drugs for dispensing in the U.S., with labeling identifying the drugs as imported and a ban on mixing them with non-imported stock [S2][S3].
It creates a licensing system for internet pharmacies, with a public list of licensed sites and a toll-free number, so consumers can verify a website is legitimate before ordering [S3].

It requires credit card companies and other payment systems to block payments to unlicensed internet pharmacies, and makes ad platforms liable for ads from unlicensed pharmacies or ads claiming prescriptions aren't needed — attacks on the counterfeit-drug market [S2][S3].
It gives the FDA new tools to detain or temporarily hold drug shipments that pose a public health risk, and to suspend importation of a drug or importer that violates the rules [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the main cost, since cheaper parallel imports erode their highest-priced market. Payment processors and internet advertising companies would bear new compliance and liability costs. The FDA's enforcement work would be paid in part through fees on importers and internet pharmacy licensees [S3].

drawbacks.text: The personal-importation right is narrow: it excludes controlled substances, biologics, intravenous and infused drugs, drugs made through biotechnology, refrigerated drugs, and photoreactive drugs, so many newer treatments are not covered [S3].

Even safety supporters acknowledge the core objection: once drugs move through foreign supply chains outside FDA custody, the agency cannot fully vouch for every package, which is why the bill leans heavily on labeling, advance-shipment notices, port inspections, and detention authority — tools with real limits [S3].

The bill gives the Secretary sweeping power to suspend importation of a drug, an importer, or even an entire country's shipments, with no judicial review of those orders — broad discretion that could shut off supply unpredictably [S3].
Licensing fees, registration, and advance-notice paperwork would add costs for pharmacies and importers, some of which could be passed to consumers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers paying U.S. prices, the benefit is real and direct: the same FDA-approved pills at Canadian prices. The bill's drafters took the safety objection seriously — it is one of the most heavily regulated importation proposals, with licensing, labeling, advance notice, detention, and payment-blocking provisions — but the exclusions are broad and the suspension powers are sweeping, so the design is not costless. The genuine tradeoff is between lower prices and the difficulty of policing a supply chain the FDA does not control.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health subcommittee in February 2005, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeb Bradley of New Hampshire introduced the Safe IMPORT Act on February 10, 2005; it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
On February 25, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health — the last action recorded for the bill [S5].
No cosponsors signed on in either party [S4].
No further action appears in the record, and the 109th Congress ended January 3, 2007, so the bill died in subcommittee without a hearing or vote [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: without importation, they kept selling the same FDA-approved drugs at the higher U.S. prices, and American patients kept paying them. Rogue internet pharmacies also kept operating without the licensing regime that would have exposed them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers kept U.S. prices

for.name: Rep. Jeb Bradley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor

against.name: House Subcommittee on Health (Energy and Commerce)
against.role: Subcommittee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 25, 2005 and never scheduled a hearing or markup; no further action was taken

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Fought drug importation legislation throughout this era through public campaigns and lobbying, arguing imported drugs could not be guaranteed safe

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no roll-call exists; the only measurable support was one Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, which makes the partisan shape unknowable from the record.

industries.note: Importation lets consumers buy the same FDA-approved drugs at Canadian prices, which are far lower because Canada negotiates or regulates prices. Every dollar shifted to a Canadian purchase is U.S. revenue lost at the higher price.

industries.industry: Licensed pharmacies, internet pharmacies, and wholesalers (including Canadian)
industries.note: Licensed importers would gain a legal market for dispensing lower-priced imported drugs, while unlicensed internet pharmacies would be shut out of payment systems and face shipment refusal. The licensed operators' gain comes from serving consumers who want cheaper drugs, so their interest runs with the public's.

industries.industry: Credit card networks and payment processors
industries.note: The bill requires federal regulators to issue rules forcing payment systems to identify and block transactions with unlicensed internet pharmacies, imposing compliance costs, though it shields them from liability for good-faith blocking.

Ad services and website hosts would face liability for accepting ads from unlicensed internet pharmacies or ads claiming no prescription is needed, and courts could order them to disable offending sites.
